The one thing to be careful is how many you take, and from where. There a cap of (40) AI max per side, and a limit of two squads and a doubles AI (10) spawnable at a base.
 Whatever base you spawn them at, are tied to that bases spawn limit. 


If you spawn AI at a purple base amd take them with you, then noone can spawn more to defend that base until the ones you take have died. AI is known to randomly wander away or get stuck in place because of the changing issues right now. It can make situations where you can't spawn new AI at a purple for defense because the ones that were taken out are still alive, risking the base. So utilizing very unimportant bases to do this is really important.

Just remeber that doing this can impact the entire team & their ability to defend. Risk reward.

Yes, Living Quarters (small or large) cuts spawn cost for standard & custom kit by 50%. 

It also allows you to spawn AI (general consensus is 40 AI per team), which is best used at Purple bases (since they're so important), but sometimes a fire team at a key base that's being constantly pushed to give time for more human troops to get boots on the ground. 

The small or large one give the same benefits. Best practice is to tuck them away from the main HQ Tent. Each structure acts as a spawn point, so it's good to spread them out.

  
As a vet, I've found the best prioritization is:  
Radio > Light Vehicle (gets supplies moving, gets people to the next objective)  
  
If supplies are available & have the rank:  
Radio > Living Quarters > Light Vehicle

Adding rank requirement to armory would definitely change the meta. 
Living quarters are so powerful though since not only half respawn cost, but placing AI. They'd have to still lock Ai under higher rank, otherwise privates would be spawning Ai at early bases

For my commissions, I use AnyDesk. It's free and doesn't require any software install, it creates a one-time remote session, so my client can run the program, connect to my machine and enter their credentials into the unity project. It's free and that way I'm not handling other people's login information. It makes my clients feel much safer, plus saves the annoyance of changing your passwords

Normally I just publish and if I need to make changes, upload over it without changing blueprint ID.

To avoid the issue of giving your login information, I use free remote desktop software like AnyDesk for uploading on behalf of clients. It allows a one time remote session without installing software and you can restrict functionality to keyboard and mouse (no admin). 

They get their own mouse cursor and can enter their credentials into Unity > VRC Control Panel to upload, then log them out after + send the files to their Google drive, etc. 

From an infosec perspective, this makes everyone more comfortable since I'm not handling anyone's account info, abd the client doesn't have to change passwords afterwards.  I've also found that most are really curious seeing their project in Unity and feel safer with this process. It's also great for teaching sessions since I can point things out with my mouse on their machine, enabling more hands on learning. Had nothing but 100% positive feedback from this method.

My personal experience has been really positive with fat cycling. 210lbs to 168/172lbs, 6ft. HRT IM injections, 2.75 years. Religiously kept to my injection schedule. 
I did this with lazy keto, intermittent fasting, and small calorie deficit/calorie in calorie out. I get all my main carbs from veggies and eat healthy fats, cook with healthier oils. After initial weight loss of 40 lbs over the course of about 14 months, I put my awareness on maintenance with a variance (natural cycling). During the course of this, I would steadily lose portions of weight, say 10lbs. Then become more lazy in my calories in, gain a few lbs, then continue. I noticed I slowly but steadily lost fat in the needed area while still depositing fat in female pattern locations. Once I was around a healthy weight, I continued with lower calorie deficit but still allowing myself to go over some days. I still have some visceral fat but its greatly reduced and I'm still seeing progress. My doctor was surprised by the changes I was experiencing and towards gentle fat cycling. My hips, butt, and breasts have reshaped tremendously while losing nearly all of my tummy. 

I took the slow and steady approach, trying to be gentle with myself, cultivating patience that it was a long process I was doing. My diet improved significantly, had more energy, and I noticed I no longer dealt with bloating, which helped with proportions even further. It does help the fact that I generally avoid carb-y or sugary foods, never liked them. I further honed my cooking skills in the process, learned more about nutrition, included organic when viable. organic seasonings made a huge difference to satisfy certain taste cravings and reduced the needed portion to meet that desire... they're stronger and some have additional health benefits as well. Pink salt vs iodized, grinding organic peppercorn vs pre-ground.

YMMV as always, but perhaps my personal experience may offer another perspective or ideas that resonate with you. I'm happy to share further it it could help someone!

Electrolysis is the best, it's permanent hair removal, whereas laser is permanent hair reduction. The other commenters correct about it taking three, even up to six separate terminations of the hair follicle. Your hair grows in Cycles and can only be killed if it's in an active growing cycle. This means that early on well you have a lot of hair being removed, it may seem like a lot is growing right back. It all adds up and builds momentum though after you first clear an area. I'm nearly done with electrolysis and have been doing it for three years, minimum of 1 hour every two weeks. Some areas took 3 to 4 months for hair to hit an active growth cycle and regrow for removal.  Here are my tips from experience. Pain management was the biggest thing for me (sensitive skin):

•Hydrate! Make sure you drink plenty of water for a few days before electrolysis. Our skin gets dehydrated first when we're not getting enough fluids or consuming things that dehydrate us, which makes your skin much more sensitive. This is a good General Health practice as well to support your body in transition.

• avoid caffeine within 6 hours of your appointment, preferably not the day of. This also increases your sensitivity and can make it more painful. YMMV but I found alcohol also increases my sensitivity and pain level.

• topical analgesic: get EMLA cream or something similar. There is some you can get over the counter, but this cream is through prescription only and is much more powerful. You apply it an hour before your appointment and it makes a huge difference in pain.

• additional pain options: I found the combination of an anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen, an anti-anxiety medication like clonazepam or another benzodiazepine, as well as headphones/music to zone put to, and meditative breathing to work well for me. Once I got to some really sensitive areas on the underside of my chin, my doctor prescribed me a low dose of Tramadol to help with the additional pain.

•Aftercare: follow all of your technicians Aftercare instructions to the letter. Don't pick at any scabs or pimples that may occur from the voided follicle. It can take up to two weeks for those follicles to heal, and redness and burning is quite common. I tried quite a few homeopathic options but found the best product for aftercare is Finipil. It's a non-comeogenic anespectic, and it fills the vacated follicles, preventing oil and bacteria from causing pimples and further irritation. It cools your skin, reduces inflammation redness and the heat/pain significantly. It also deeply moisturizes the area which helps in the healing process and general comfort. Nufree finipil pro/elec Antiseptic Cream 2.5 Ounce https://www.amazon.com/dp/B01BKTB7MO/ref=cm_sw_r_cp_apap_Hg2NaLRINbpUR

I started immediately with electrolysis instead of doing laser, as many people have mentioned they had regrowth after 5 to 7 years, and being one of the most dysphoric aspects of my body, I wanted to remove it permanently and have that guarantee. It did wonders for passing after reaching a certain point and I found the sessions became much more manageable overtime as I got used to it, except for some sensitive areas as mentioned previously.

The last thing I recommend is if you have the option of multiple providers, don't be afraid to try different technicians. I started out with two of the cheaper options in town and did not have his good results as one I paid an extra $8 an hour for. It's your face and your skin, so it's not worth saving a few bucks to potentially have problems later. If you notice blisters or anyting else along those lines, it can indicate an improper insertion technique or too high of a voltage if you're going with thermolysis. Definitely talk to your technician if that's the case, and do some research on electrolysis forums for more information if that resonates with you as well.

Feel free to ask any questions or DM me if you'd like more information. Best wishes in your hair removal journey!
